subject: bicycle
pitch: A vintage Dutch city bicycle in mint green. Tall upright handlebars with cream grips and a silver bell, a brown leather saddle with springs, chrome mudguards, a chain guard, a wicker basket on the front filled with sunflowers and a baguette, and whitewall tyres.
reasoning:
I'm planning out the bike's dimensions and orientation, then setting up a root joint since the structure needs one even without a creature attached.

For rigging, I'll keep it minimal with a steering joint, front/rear wheel joints, and a crank joint. I'm working out the rear and front axle positions, the bottom bracket location, and sketching the head tube and fork geometry using a steering angle around 70 degrees to get realistic rake and lean for a Dutch-style step-through frame.

Now I'm laying out the frame tubes themselves: fork legs running from the crown down to the front axle, a curved step-through down tube sweeping from the head tube to the bottom bracket, a seat tube rising from the bottom bracket, and chain stays and seat stays connecting to the rear axle on each side.

For the wheels, I'm thinking through torus geometry for the tire, rotated so it sits properly in the YZ plane, and considering how to add a whitewall stripe using either a second thinner torus or flat rings on the sides.

The whitewall ring approach is getting tricky since it'd sit hidden inside the torus geometry. Instead I'll paint the whitewall directly onto the torus surface using a radial-distance-based paint function keyed off each wheel's center position.

For the rim and spokes, I'll add a smaller chrome torus plus thin rod geometries connecting hub to rim, keeping part counts in check given the overall limit.

For the hub cylinder, I'm rotating it 90 degrees around z to align it horizontally. For the mudguards, I'm working out how to orient a partial torus arc so its axis points along world x, rotating the torus geometry around y first so it lies flat in the YZ plane before scaling.

Now I'm tracing through the math of where each point on the arc ends up after that rotation, figuring out which angle corresponds to the front of the fender so I can define the correct arc span for covering the wheel from front to top.

The front fender arc runs from about 60° to 200° (140° span), and the rear fender covers roughly -20° to 120° (also 140°), both centered on the wheel position. I'm also scaling the torus tube width by 2.2 in x to make the fender wide enough (about 0.088), with the fender radius set to 0.375 matching the wheel center.

Now I'm working out the drivetrain side (right, -X direction since left is +X), positioning the chainring at x=-0.08. For the chain guard, I'm planning a teardrop-shaped extrusion covering the chainring and rear sprocket, running from the bottom bracket to the rear axle, using an extrude direction setup where the default forward axis crosses with up to give the thickness along -x.

Still plotting guard outline points...

I'll make the chain guard mint-colored, skip adding a visible chainring since it's hidden, and add crank arms and pedals as separate rod-and-box geometry positioned at the bottom bracket with offsets on either side.

For a modest rear rack, I'll place a flat box above the rear fender with small struts connecting to the axle, keeping it minimal. Then I'll add a brown leather saddle and a chrome seat post running from the frame up to the seat.

Shaping saddle profile stations...

Adding chrome rail rods from the seat clamp to the saddle bottom, then moving on to the handlebars: a tall upright Dutch-style stem rising from the head tube along the steering axis to around y≈1.12 before sweeping back.

Still working out the handlebar geometry...

Still working out the handlebar curve points...

Now I'm adding small details: brake lever rods extending forward from the grips, and a bell mounted on the bar made from a hemisphere dome on a small base cylinder, positioned near the left grip.

I'm also considering a front headlamp near the head tube, then shifting focus to the front basket—sizing and centering it above the front wheel on the rack, accounting for wheel height so it sits properly without overlapping.

I'm working out how to mount the basket to the fork with silver support rods running from the fork crown and dropouts up to the basket's base, mimicking a real rack attachment. For the basket itself I'm thinking of a woven wicker look using a flared rectangular frustum shape.

Building basket walls as simple box panels...

Now I'm adding a top rim of rods with corner spheres and arched wicker handles on each side, then setting up the sunflower contents with stems and petal-ring heads positioned inside the basket.

Still writing petal geometry...

Working out positions for each flower head so they cluster above the basket, leaning outward with varying forward-up facing directions and bases rooted near the basket rim.

Checking that the fifth flower position keeps enough spacing from the others and adjusting its direction, then adding a few green teardrop leaves near the basket rim. For the baguette, I'm working out a diagonal placement resting across the basket so it doesn't overlap with the flowers already positioned there.

I'm reworking the basket layout to put flowers on the left cluster and the baguette angled out on the right side, adjusting coordinates until the lengths and positions look plausible relative to the frame.

I'm routing the baguette between the two points, checking it clears nearby flowers with enough margin, then working out a tapered geometry with gold coloring and diagonal scoring slashes to mimic bread crust.

Still working out the slash geometry...

Now I'm thinking through the loft shape for the basket with tapered width stations from narrow at the ends to wider in the middle, using smooth catmull interpolation with rounded caps. I'm deciding to skip adding a headlamp near the fork crown to keep things simple.

Adding a small red reflector on the rear fender and a tiny rear light box. I'm considering a ring lock on the seat stays like Dutch bikes have, but deciding to skip it in favor of a folded center stand with two angled rods running from behind the bottom bracket down toward the rear wheel area.

Now I'm computing coordinates for the stand rods and a cross rod so they fold up without dipping below the ground plane, then working out fender stay rods connecting the axles to the front and rear fenders using the wheel's angular position to place the attachment point correctly.

I'm checking for clashes between the fender and tire geometry — the fender's inner radius was coming in smaller than the tire's outer radius, so I'm adjusting the fender radius and tube thickness to keep clearance.

Now I'm checking whether the seat tube passes through the rear fender near the top, tracing the seat tube's z-position at the fender's y-height to see if they overlap.

Next I'm tracing the seat stays from the seat tube down to the rear axle, checking their x-offset against the fender and tire width to confirm they clear without intersecting.

I'm reworking the stay geometry so they offset outward near the seat cluster and taper toward the axle, keeping clear of the tire and fender width by just a few millimeters of margin.

Still working out the fork leg placement so they clear the front wheel circle, angling from the crown down to the axle with a slight outward taper and a small leg radius for proportion.

Now I'm setting up the fender support stays connecting the axle to the fender edges, then moving on to the tire's paint logic and the skeleton of joint positions—root, steer, and the rest of the frame hierarchy—to anchor everything together.

Still defining joint hierarchy...

I'll switch to using capsules for frame tubes so joints get rounded caps instead of flat ones, and I'm plotting the down tube's curve from the head tube down to the bottom bracket with intermediate control points, considering whether to add a second diagonal tube like on a traditional step-through frame.

Deciding against a second diagonal and keeping just the single sweeping tube plus seat tube, with a radius around 0.026 for an elegant look. I'm positioning a head tube capsule and adding a small head badge decal as a tilted disc near the front of the head tube.

I'm skipping cream frame stripes and visible chainring details for simplicity, keeping fenders chrome and the chain hidden behind a guard. Now I'm placing chrome headset rings at the head tube ends and sketching the stem geometry as a chrome rod running up to the handlebar clamp, working out the steering axis direction for proper alignment.

Checking the stem's continuation from the head tube top, I'm adjusting the handlebar centre point and recalculating the bar curve coordinates to match the head tube slope, then verifying the fork steer axis stays consistent through the frame with a bit of rake offset.

The fork leg needs a straight bend from crown to axle for proper rake geometry, which checks out with the slope I calculated. I'll skip the brake levers since the geometry is getting too fiddly, and just add simple rod shapes for them instead.

Now I'm positioning the rear fender end and figuring out its downward curve and relative z/y coordinates, along with checking the overall front-to-rear length of the bike.

I'm placing the small red rear reflector box on the fender at an appropriate angle and radius, confirming it stays within the bike's z-extent, then sketching the rear rack platform dimensions above the fender's top height.

For the rack, I'm defining its chrome plate position and spanning length, then adding support struts: rear rods connecting the rack's back corners down to the axle, and front rods connecting the rack's front edge up toward the seat tube/stay area, checking that these rods clear the fender width and tire.

Now I'm placing the pedals as small flat boxes with crank arms, positioning the right pedal center at x=-0.17 and left at x=0.125, then calculating crank arm lengths and angles connecting the bottom bracket to each pedal, with the left crank extended higher and the right lower-forward, plus a bottom bracket axle rod running across.

I'm positioning the chainring guard at x=-0.09 with a .02 width, checking it clears the chain stay and doesn't overlap the rear wheel plane, and extending it back near the rear axle hub with bolts, considering a mint color with cream edge detailing.

Now I'm checking the seat tube and seat post alignment, tracing the slope to find where the seat tube meets the post, then working out the saddle rail geometry—placing the rear rails near z=-0.46 and the nose near z=-0.22, with the saddle sitting about 0.03 above the clamp.

Saddle spans from -0.52 to -0.17 in length. I want to add a countershaded leather color to the saddle, brighter on top and darker underneath, plus a couple small brass rivet spheres near the nose for detail.

For the springs, I'm using the spiral path helper to coil chrome wire around a center axis near the saddle, setting the pitch and turn count, then sweeping a thin tube along that path with a small radius bound to the root bone.

Now I'm setting up the wheels: a hub point, a chrome rim made from a rotated torus, and a tire torus with whitewall paint applied based on distance from the hub and the surface normal to mark the sidewall ring.

I'll settle on a whitewall band defined by d between 0.322 and 0.350 with |n.x|>0.5, using 10 radial and 48 tubular segments for the torus tire, painted white "#f4efe2". For the hub, I'm adding a chrome cylinder with flange discs and skipping tread bumps and valve details, then moving on to the front dynamo hub.

Spokes get modeled as thin rods connecting hub points to crossing rim points at 12 positions per side, using a tiny radius around 0.0025 for visibility at low poly. For the mudguard I'm realizing TorusGeometry doesn't support a thetaStart parameter, only an arc length starting at zero, so I need to rotate the geometry afterward to get the correct starting angle instead.

Working out the rotation math for positioning the fenders...

I'm checking that the fender's rear end near the head tube doesn't clash with the fork crown or legs — the clearances look fine with the current spacing. I'll skip the pinstripe detail and move on to the fender stay rods connecting to the fork.

Now I'm working out the stay geometry from the axle to the fender at various angles around the arc, checking which points give realistic stay positions without the angles ending up too far forward.

Then I move on to the rear fender stays, placing them from the rear axle to fender at a shallow angle, and bridging the top with seat stays. After that I'm sketching kickstand placement and lamp position, then switching to the basket geometry -- positioning its walls and bottom plate, the rack platform beneath it, and the support rods connecting the rack to the fork crown.

I check the rod from the rack to the front axle to make sure it clears the tire and fender, confirming the offset is wide enough. Then I think about the wicker weave paint function, wanting a shared pattern logic that alternates tones based on position so it reads correctly on both the side walls and the front wall depending on which coordinate varies.

Now I'm sketching the basket rim rods, corner edges, and handle geometry, defining capsule arcs that curve up from the rim to form the handle loops on each side.

I'm worried handles might overlap the flower petals near the edge, so I'm considering skipping handles altogether and refining a flower-building function that derives a local basis from the stem direction to orient the petals properly.

Now I'm detailing the flower geometry itself: pointed star-shaped petals in two layered colors (gold and orange-yellow) offset slightly for depth, a dark brown disc center, a lighter inner ring, and green sepals behind for a natural layered look.

Still building the stem and leaf shapes, working out the star-point vertex math for petal extrusion and sketching teardrop leaf outlines...

Placing a few leaves around the rim with droop directions and side vectors, planning a helper function that extrudes each leaf shape given its position and direction.

Now I'm figuring out the baguette as a swept shape along a curved path, then placing the bell near the handlebar base using its coordinate position.

I'm deciding to skip the striker rod and headlamp details since they'd conflict with the basket and fender geometry, keeping things simple with just the mint "#86d0b0" main color and no extra decals or two-tone bands.

Now I'm working out the joint hierarchy — the steering joint at the head tube parents the front wheel, cranks attach at the bottom bracket, and I need to make sure joints get created before parts reference their bones. I'm also checking overall proportions so the model sits properly with wheels touching ground level, then wrapping up with the default export returning the root bone.

Checking the torus geometry math confirms the tire bottoms essentially touch the ground. Now I'm setting up imports from the builder library and need to resolve a naming conflict where `mix` is exported from both the paint and context modules.

Writing joint hierarchy...

Writing wheel geometry logic...

Checking the chain guard geometry for clashes with the crank arm, chain stay, and rear hub positions to make sure nothing overlaps.

I'm skipping extra decorative details like a bezel stripe or logo oval to keep things simple, and setting up the kickstand rods with proper placement relative to the chain stay and bottom bracket. Now I'm defining the wicker basket walls as boxes attached to the steering bone, then moving on to paint the final geometry.

Working out basket dimensions, rim rods, and flower stem placements before finalizing the build and returning the root object.
